title: Comments or, in the Alternative, Limited Protest of Appalachian Voices in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 02/23/2026 compliance filing proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff under ER26-1479.

documents.name: ER26-1479-000 Comment of Appalachian Voices.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                                     Docket No. ER26-1479-000

              COMMENTS OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LIMITED PROTEST
                          OF APPALACHIAN VOICES

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC or

Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Appalachian Voices submits these comments or,

in the alternative, limited protest in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) compliance

filing proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (Tariff) concerning co-located

load (Compliance Filing).2 The Compliance Filing addresses the Commission’s directives in its

December 18, 2025 order in Docket No. EL25-49-000, et al.3 (Order Directing Compliance) by

proposing, among other things, to revise the Tariff provisions applicable to retail Behind-the-

Meter Generation (BTMG). For the avoidance of doubt, Appalachian Voices submits these

comments to seek clarification that the Compliance Filing’s proposed 50 MW materiality

threshold for BTMG applies to the aggregate capacity of all generation resources at a single

customer site, rather than to each individual generating unit. If PJM intended that this threshold

apply only to individual units, Appalachian Voices urges the Commission to reject this aspect of

the Compliance Filing and direct further compliance.

I.      BACKGROUND

        The proliferation of data centers has raised difficult questions about the impacts their

interconnection and the associated generation they require will have on other users of the grid,

 particularly in the PJM region. To address some of these challenges, the Commission issued an

order on February 20, 2025, directing PJM to show cause as to why its Tariff remains just and

reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without specific provisions addressing

service to co-location arrangements between large loads and generators.4 In response to public

comment, the Commission issued the Order Directing Compliance on December 18, 2025,

directing PJM to revise its Tariff to set forth specific terms and conditions for customers seeking

to interconnect load co-located with generation.5

        The Commission’s compliance directives included a requirement that PJM revise its

Tariff provisions related to retail BTMG. PJM’s Tariff defines BTMG as “a generation unit that

delivers energy to load without using the Transmission System or any distribution facilities[.]”6

Currently, the Tariff allows load serving entities that serve loads with BTMG to reduce their level

of service and the associated costs by netting output from the BTMG in the calculation of their

peak demand for the purpose of determining Network Integration Transmission Service charges.7

        In its Order Directing Compliance, the Commission found that changed circumstances

have made PJM’s existing Tariff provisions unjust and unreasonable, citing PJM’s own

conclusion that the existing rules were “conceived for, and [have] been implemented for,

substantially smaller loads . . . and not on the scale of large data centers.”8 Again echoing PJM,

the Commission noted that “[a]llowing very large loads like data centers to net is problematic

because loads in this configuration do not carry reserves.”9 Yet, because load serving entities

must nevertheless serve these loads, the current rules would allow these loads to “lean on the

 PJM system when the co-located generation is on a full or partial outage or if the load exceeds

the rating of the co-located generation.”10 The Commission concluded, therefore, that because

PJM’s existing rules do not limit the amount of qualifying load that a Network Customer may net

by using BTMG, PJM’s operative Tariff provisions “are no longer consistent with cost causation

principles, because large loads configured in a BTMG arrangement with significant generation

will raise cost shifting concerns compared to loads pursuing smaller amounts of netting.”11 The

Commission concluded that this could create reliability and resource adequacy risks.

         As a result, the Commission directed PJM to revise the BTMG provisions in its Tariff.12

The Commission acknowledged, however, that not all loads using BTMG are large enough to

create reliability and resource adequacy risks. The Commission therefore directed PJM “to

propose a new MW threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that

Network Customers may net by using” BTMG.13

         On February 23, 2026, PJM submitted its Compliance Filing. As relevant here, in its

transmittal letter, PJM proposed “to establish a materiality threshold of up to 50 MW for a

generator at the same electrical location as the Network Load for generation units to qualify as

Retail BTMG.”14 PJM proposed the following Tariff language to effectuate its materiality

threshold: “‘Retail Behind The Meter Generation’ shall refer to Behind The Meter Generation

that is used to serve a retail load served by a Network Customer located at the same electrical

location, where such generation has a cumulative nameplate rating of no greater than 50

MW[.]”15

 II.      COMMENTS OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LIMITED PROTEST

         PJM’s proposed Tariff language sets the materiality threshold for BTMG at “a cumulative

nameplate rating of no greater than 50 MW[.]”16 This would appear to subject all generation at a

single customer site to a collective threshold of 50 MW for BTMG purposes, in keeping with the

Order Directing Compliance’s requirements. However, PJM’s transmittal letter injects

uncertainty into this application by stating that the 50 MW threshold applies to “a generator at

the same electrical location as the Network Load[.]”17 These equivocal descriptions make it

unclear whether PJM intends the 50 MW threshold to apply to the aggregate nameplate ratings of

all generation at a single site or only to each individual generator at the same electrical location

as network load.

         Applying the latter interpretation would undermine the Commission’s purpose in

requiring a materiality threshold in the first place. The Commission required PJM to propose a

materiality threshold “because large loads configured in a BTMG arrangement with significant

generation will raise cost shifting concerns compared to loads pursuing smaller amounts of

netting[,]”18 which, in turn, could create reliability and resource adequacy risks. Applying the 50

MW materiality threshold separately to multiple, individual BTMG facilities at the same

electrical location as Network Load would not address this concern. It would create a loophole

whereby load co-located with significant generation in the form of several generators under 50

MW could subtract their collective nameplate capacity from its peak load and effectively operate

outside the constraints and oversight PJM proposes in the rest of its compliance filing. This

the Network Load[.]”).
18

                                                          4
 would unjustly and unreasonably shift costs and exacerbate the reliability and resource adequacy

risks the Commission has already identified.

         Accordingly, for the avoidance of doubt, Appalachian Voices seeks clarification that

PJM’s proposed Tariff language would establish a materiality threshold for Retail BTMG of no

more than 50 MW, inclusive of all generation at the same electrical location, despite the

ambiguous language in its transmittal letter.19 In the alternative, to the extent PJM’s proposed

materiality threshold of 50 MW would apply individually to multiple generators at the same

electrical location, Appalachian Voices requests that the Commission reject PJM’s proposal and

require further compliance.

III.     CONCLUSION

         For the foregoing reasons, Appalachian Voices respectfully requests the clarification

described above. In the alternative, Appalachian Voices respectfully asks that the Commission

reject this aspect of PJM’s Compliance Filing and require further compliance.
